paragraphs.heading: What a solvable group is
paragraphs.text: In group theory, a solvable group, also called a soluble group, is one that can be built up from abelian groups by extensions. An equivalent test uses the derived series: take the commutator subgroup, then the commutator subgroup of that, and so on. The group is solvable when this chain eventually reaches the trivial subgroup, and the fewest steps needed is called its derived length.

paragraphs.heading: Finite groups and radicals
paragraphs.text: For finite groups there is another equivalent description: a group is solvable if it has a composition series whose factors are all cyclic groups of prime order. The Jordan–Hölder theorem ensures that if one composition series has this property, every composition series does. When the group is the Galois group of a polynomial, those cyclic pieces correspond to nth roots, or radicals, over some field.

paragraphs.heading: Examples
paragraphs.text: Abelian groups are the basic examples, and they are solvable in a trivial way, since the group itself and the trivial group already form the needed series. Non-abelian groups may or may not be solvable. All nilpotent groups are solvable, so finite p-groups are too. The symmetric group S₃ is a small example that is solvable but not nilpotent.

paragraphs.heading: Big theorems
paragraphs.text: The alternating group of degree 5, A₅, is the smallest simple non-abelian group, so every group with fewer than 60 elements is solvable. The Feit–Thompson theorem says every finite group of odd order is solvable. Burnside's theorem says a finite group of order p^aqᵇ, with p and q prime and a and b non-negative integers, is solvable too.

paragraphs.heading: Closure rules
paragraphs.text: Every subgroup of a solvable group is solvable, and so is any group that a solvable group maps onto by a homomorphism. Going the other way, if a normal subgroup N and the quotient G/N are both solvable, then G is solvable. As a result, the direct product of two solvable groups is solvable.

paragraphs.heading: Why equations care
paragraphs.text: For n > 4 the symmetric group Sₙ is not solvable, using the fact that its subgroup Aₙ is normal, maximal, simple and non-abelian. This is a key step in proving the Abel–Ruffini theorem: for every n > 4 some polynomials of degree n cannot be solved by radicals. The same property is also used in complexity theory, where it helps prove Barrington's theorem.
